title: The Mineral Revolution: Gold and Migrant Labour
summary: The discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand, the growth of Johannesburg, deep-level mining and the Randlords, the migrant labour system, pass laws and the road to the South African War.

notes.text: In **1886** gold was found on the farm Langlaagte on the **Witwatersrand** in the South African Republic (ZAR, the Transvaal), ruled by President **Paul Kruger**. The Witwatersrand had the largest gold deposits in the world, but the gold was spread thinly through hard rock, deep underground.

Within ten years a mining camp grew into **Johannesburg**, a city of about 100 000 people: the largest town in southern Africa. Fortune-seekers came from all over the world. Many foreign (mostly British) miners and businessmen were called **uitlanders** (foreigners) by the Boers.

items: Gold-bearing reef sloped deep underground, so expensive **deep-level mining** was needed.
Huge amounts of rock had to be crushed, and cyanide was used from 1890 to extract the gold.
Only wealthy mining companies could afford this. Their owners, such as Rhodes, Alfred Beit and Julius Wernher, were called **Randlords**.
In 1889 mine owners formed the **Chamber of Mines**, which agreed to keep black wages low and recruit workers together.

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: The price of gold was fixed internationally, so mine owners could not raise prices to cover their high costs. Instead, they kept **labour costs as low as possible**. This is the main reason for the system of cheap migrant labour.
A system in which workers leave their homes to work far away for a contract period, then return home, while their families stay behind.

Black men were recruited from rural areas of South Africa and from Mozambique, Lesotho, Botswana and Malawi. They signed contracts of 6 to 18 months, lived in single-sex **compounds** (hostels) and sent money home. Many were forced into this work by **taxes** (such as the hut tax) that had to be paid in cash, and by laws that limited African land ownership.

rows: Men away for long periods; women, children and the elderly did all the farm work
Dangerous, hot, deep underground work; rock falls and explosions
Lung diseases such as silicosis and TB, spread when men returned home

notes.text: **Pass laws** forced black men to carry a document (a **pass**) showing who they worked for and where they could be. Without a valid pass a worker could be arrested. Passes helped mine owners control workers and stopped them from leaving for better-paying jobs. Pass laws were extended over the next century and became one of the most hated parts of segregation and apartheid.

items: Britain wanted control of the gold-rich Transvaal. Kruger's government taxed the mines and refused the vote to uitlanders.
In **1895–1896** the **Jameson Raid**, backed by Rhodes, tried and failed to overthrow Kruger's government.
Tension led to the **South African War (Anglo-Boer War) of 1899–1902**, after which the Boer republics became British colonies.
In **1910** the colonies were united as the **Union of South Africa**, in which only white men could vote in most of the country.
